description: Programmable cryptography explained at the pace of a 2009 MSN chat: 2PC and garbled circuits, SNARKs, FHE, and ORAM as one toolkit. A fair-use walkthrough of the 0xPARC primer, with a live SHA-256 preimage demo.
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. Hash a secret in the demo above.
disclosure: How to read this: a first-pass walkthrough of "Programmable Cryptography: Four Easy Pieces" by Evan Chen, Brian Lawrence, and Yan X Zhang (0xPARC, 2025), summarized under fair use with credit. The learner lines and pacing are AI; the SHA-256 demo hashes for real.

editorial.reader: A curious reader who knows the surface term but wants the mechanism.
editorial.problem: The reader can recognize pcrypto vocabulary without being able to predict what its mechanism will do.
editorial.thesis: The page should leave the reader able to explain pcrypto in plain language and predict its behavior.
evidence: The conversation cites its sources and the demos make the mechanism visible.
The understanding check names common misconceptions and explains every answer.
editorial.uncertainty: The demos teach the model; they do not replace a measurement or a full treatment.

understanding.intro: Before you close the window: pop quiz, 5 questions, no grades. The demo up there keeps hashing if you need it.

questions.q: Start with the word itself. What separates second-generation, programmable cryptography from the first generation?

options.t: gen 1 hand-built one protocol per problem, gen 2 gives primitives you can program for any function
options.why: Right. RSA signs a message and the millionaire problem got its own bespoke protocol; second-generation primitives take any function you can write as code, and you compile the problem you have.

options.t: gen 2 runs on blockchains, that's where the programmable part comes in
options.why: Blockchains arrive at the end of the story, as the demand that pulled the practical work forward. The definition lives up top: primitives you can program for any function, no chain required.

options.t: gen 1 was hardware, gen 2 does the same jobs in software
options.why: The alarm-clock-to-smartphone line is an analogy about generality. Both generations are software; the jump it describes is from single-purpose tools to a general-purpose one.

options.t: gen 2 crypto can be patched and upgraded after it ships
options.why: Programmable here means the primitive takes an arbitrary function as its input, the way a computer takes a program. It promises nothing about updating algorithms already deployed.

questions.q: Two millionaires settle who earns more with the 2PC protocol from this chat. What does each of them actually get to see?

options.t: both learn who won and nothing else, via a circuit one side garbles and the other evaluates blind
options.why: That's the 2PC promise: each party keeps their input and both get only F(x1, x2). The garbled circuit plus oblivious transfer is the engine, and past two parties this grows into MPC.

options.t: a trusted referee collects both incomes and announces the winner
options.why: That's exactly the setup 2PC deletes. Nobody ever holds both inputs: the boolean circuit gets evaluated gate by gate on encrypted values, so there's no middleman to trust or to leak.

options.t: the winner gets to learn the loser's income, the loser learns nothing
options.why: Neither side learns the other's number, whichever way it goes. The output is the single bit of who earns more, and both parties see exactly that and no more.

options.t: they swap encrypted incomes and each decrypts the other's copy locally
options.why: If either side could decrypt the other's income the privacy would be gone. The trick is computing on values neither party can open alone: one garbles the circuit, the other evaluates it blind.

questions.q: The demo above hashes your secret M and prints sha256(M) live. What would a real SNARK add on top of what the demo already does?

options.t: a proof that i know some M behind that exact digest, without ever showing M
options.why: That's the statement shape from the chat: I know X such that F(X, Y) = Z, with F and the digest public and only the witness hidden. The demo gives you the public half; the SNARK adds the proof of knowledge.

options.t: it would encrypt the digest so nobody else can read the hash
options.why: The digest stays public on purpose: it's the reference a verifier checks the proof against. Secrecy covers only the witness M, the thing you typed into the box.

options.t: it would let the verifier run sha256 backwards and recover M
options.why: Nobody recovers M; that would defeat the exercise. The verifier ends up convinced you know a preimage while learning nothing about it, which is the whole trick the demo is teeing up.

options.t: it would swap in a faster hash so the proof is cheap to make
options.why: F stays whatever the statement needs, here SHA-256 encoded as equations. And proving stays expensive: the chat's number is millions of times the cost of just running the computation.

questions.q: Suppose your records sit on a server fully encrypted, FHE-style, and the server can read none of them. What is left for ORAM to hide?

options.t: which records i touch, how often, and which ones together
options.why: The access pattern leaks even when every byte is ciphertext. ORAM scrambles each request into a batch of reads and writes so the server can't tell which one you actually wanted.

options.t: the key, in case the server tries to brute-force the ciphertext
options.why: ORAM assumes the encryption already holds. The leak it plugs is behavioral: the server watching which ciphertexts you ask for, how often, and in what company.

options.t: my ip address, so the server can't tell who's connecting
options.why: Hiding who connects is a network-layer job for tools like Tor. ORAM's server knows exactly who you are; what it can't learn is which of your records a request was really for.

options.t: nothing much, it's a caching layer that speeds up encrypted reads
options.why: The RAM in the name fools people. ORAM spends extra reads and writes per request to bury the real one, so it pays performance to buy privacy.

questions.q: Last one. If this toolkit can compute on secrets and prove any statement you can encode, why did it spend a decade as mostly theory?

options.t: the overhead, proving a computation can cost millions of times just running it
options.why: The primer is blunt about that number. It stayed mostly theory until blockchains and other decentralized systems demanded it hard enough to pull the practical work forward.

options.t: it needs special trusted chips that most servers didn't have yet
options.why: Backwards: this toolkit exists so you never have to trust a chip. Every guarantee here comes from protocols and math; betting on trusted hardware is the TEE, the far end of the spectrum.

options.t: the math was never proven secure so nobody dared to deploy it
options.why: The theory was the mature half; constructions existed for years. Implementation is what lagged, because the costs were brutal until real demand showed up.

options.t: encoding programs as equations stayed an unsolved research problem
options.why: Turning F into equations is standard machinery, it's how the SNARK statement gets built at all. The bottleneck was the sheer cost of proving, and demand is what finally moved it.

messages.html: people keep saying "programmable cryptography" like it's one thing. RSA is cryptography, MPC is cryptography. what's the second word doing?

0xPARC coined it for the second generation of crypto, roughly the last 15 years. First-generation crypto hand-builds a protocol per problem: RSA signs a message, and Yao's millionaire problem gets its own bespoke protocol to compare two incomes. Second-generation crypto hands you primitives you can program for any function you can write as code.

Their analogy: it's the jump from single-purpose hardware (a digital alarm clock) to a general-purpose one (a smartphone that runs whatever you compile for it). You stop inventing a new algorithm per problem and start compiling the problem you have.

The primer picks four: 2PC (two-party computation), SNARKs (succinct proofs), FHE (compute on encrypted data), and ORAM (hide which data you touch). Two of those already have rooms here, so I'll wire them up as we go.

Two people compute F(x1, x2) where each knows only their own input, and neither learns the other's. Yao's millionaire problem is the classic: F is "who earns more," the inputs are the two incomes, and both walk away knowing the winner but not the number. The engine underneath is a garbled circuit (one party encrypts a boolean circuit gate by gate, the other evaluates it blind) plus oblivious transfer. Scale 2PC past two parties and you land on the MPC one room over.
you keep saying proofs. what's a SNARK?

Read a signature as a proof: Alice's signature proves "I know Alice's private key." A SNARK generalizes that to a proof of any statement shaped like "I know X such that F(X, Y) = Z," with F, Y, Z public, once you encode F as equations. The primer's headline example is "I know M such that sha(M) = Y." PLONK is one such scheme. Try the hash half live:

messages.html: so the hash is public but the M behind it stays secret. and FHE + ORAM?

FHE you've met: encrypt your data, let a server compute on the ciphertext, decrypt the result, and the server reads nothing. The primer's example is private machine translation: send Enc(x), get back Enc(translation). ORAM is the piece with no room here yet. Even with the data encrypted, the server still watches your access pattern: which records you read, how often, which ones together. Oblivious RAM scrambles each request into a batch of reads and writes, so the server can't tell which one you actually wanted.
if it does all that, why isn't it everywhere?

Cost, and the primer is blunt about it: proving a computation in a SNARK can run millions of times the cost of just doing the computation. For a decade it was mostly theory with little implementation, until blockchains and other decentralized systems started demanding it and pulled the practical work forward.
so the throughline is: one toolkit, privacy and proofs from math instead of trusted hardware.

That's the frame. 2PC and MPC, SNARKs, FHE, and ORAM are different tools, but each earns its guarantee from protocols and math rather than a chip you have to trust, the far end from a TEE. Same goal, compute on data nobody should see, with a different bet on where the trust lives.

got it. the four pieces are one compiler target, not four gadgets. thanks.
